title: Chapter 112 – Mu's Choice
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Elder Mu]

Three days before the new moon.

Elder Mu has kept the Rule for forty-one years, and in all that time he has never once read it in the dark.

He reads it now. The Law Pavilion is empty at this hour, and the lamps along the pool have burned down to a dull amber glow. He sits alone at the long table on the Council Floor with the Founders' Rule open before him, the old vellum spread flat under his palms, and he reads Article forty-four by the light of a single wick.

The Gate Bearer shall retain the right of the stair only while his standing in the Silver Leaf ranking is among the first ten.

It is a good clause. He knew it for a good clause when he read it in the spring, at the Court's table, over Zhou's soft pleasant shoulder. Plain words. A clear measure. A rule that does not ask who the man is, only where he stands. It is exactly the kind of rule Mu has spent his life defending.

He has read it forty times since the spring, and each time something in it has seemed a little more like a splinter under a fingernail.

He closes the vellum. His face in the dark pool is long and gray, with a hard mouth and a pair of deep-set eyes the color of old iron. He is seventy-three. He has outlived two Sect Heads, one wife, and a son. He is not a man accustomed to doubt.

Who wrote it?

The question has been circling for weeks. He cannot make it go away. A clause amending the Rule must be entered by an Elder of the Court, sealed with the Court's seal, and witnessed. He has checked the entry. It is in order. The Court's seal is on it. The witnesses are named. The hand that wrote the text is a clerk's: smooth, even, nondescript.

But he has not been able to find which Elder proposed it. The roll says only by resolution of the Court. And Mu, who sits on the Court, who has sat on it for forty years, has no memory of any such resolution.

* * *

The boy who brings the paper is called Lin Feng.

He comes at dawn, to the door of Mu's private study, in the plain gray of a Court runner with a jade pin in his hair. He is twenty-nine, broad and square, with his father's jaw and a Foundation Middle's slow measured breath. He carries a flat leather case, and when Mu opens the door he bows from the waist, hands at his sides, with the unhurried precision of a man who has been taught to bow by someone who meant it.

Mu knows the face. It is not the face he sees in dreams. It is, however, the face of that family: that stubborn square Lin jaw, the same deep-set eyes.

Zhao Lin, he thinks, before he can stop himself. She was fifteen.

He had called it a test. That was the word in the roll. A standard assessment of a Zhao girl of fifteen, with a suspected trace of an unregistered bloodline; the Rule allows such things in cases of doubt. He had signed the order himself. He had stood in the cold yard and watched. And when the girl's meridians had begun to burn and the examiners had looked at him, he had said, Continue, because the Rule says a test is completed.

It took her three hours to die. He has counted the minutes every night for seven years.

"Elder," says Feng, evenly. "I bring a Court petition from the Gate Bearer, sealed and witnessed. I am instructed to place it in your hand and wait for your answer."

"Instructed by whom?"

"By the Gate Bearer. And by Elder Qin Hao, who witnessed it." The young man's eyes do not waver. "I am also instructed to say that the document is true in every particular, and that the Gate Bearer will answer for it under the Rule."

Mu takes the case. His hands are steady. They have always been steady.

He breaks the seal and reads.

It is a plain document, written in a clear, regular hand, on the Court's own form. It runs to two pages. It does not accuse. It states, in order: that a note of invitation has been left on a child's desk in the Sutra Hall school; that the note is written on plum-bark paper with a blank black seal; that it summons the Gate Bearer to the Cloud Peak Annex on the night of the new moon, alone, in return for the lifting of his suspension; that the Annex is a storehouse on the north terrace belonging, by the Hall of Weights' ledger, to the Treasury; and that the Treasury has paid, for twelve months, a sum of sixty silver monthly to the bearer from a purse whose use the Gate Bearer cannot account for.

At the end, in the same careful hand: The Gate Bearer requests the Court's escort to the Annex on the night in question, and the Court's inspection of its contents, under Article twelve.

Mu reads it twice. Then he sets it on the desk, carefully, as one sets down a thing that might break.

"You have read this?" he asks.

"I carried it, Elder. I did not read it."

"Do you know what it says?"

"I know that it is true." Feng's voice is quite level. "I know that my brother could have walked into the Annex alone, and did not. He chose to put it in writing instead. He said you would understand why."

Mu looks up sharply.

"He said," Feng continues, very evenly, "that the Elder of Law is the one man in the Sect who has never once done a wrong thing under the cover of a rule. And that if the Rule is to be broken, it should be broken by the Rule itself."

For a moment the study is silent.

"That is a very clever thing to say to me," says Mu at last.

"Yes, Elder. I thought so too."

"Do you know who I am?"

"I know who you were," says Feng quietly, "to Zhao Lin."

* * *

He had not expected that.

He sits very still. The lamp ticks. Outside, in the courtyard, a bird begins to sing, and the sun makes a thin gold bar across the floor. The young man in front of him does not move, does not flinch, does not look away.

Mu's first thought is that he should have the boy flogged.

His second is that he should have himself flogged first.

"Zhao Lin was not of your blood," he says.

"The Zhao survivors are in our roll now. The girl you tested is ours in every way a roll can say." Feng's tone does not change. "I was not there. I was sent for in the morning, to help carry her out."

"I—"

"I do not say it to wound you, Elder." The young man draws a slow breath. "I say it because the Gate Bearer asked me to carry this to you, and not to the Arbiter, and not to the Court. And I wanted to know why. And when I thought about it, it seemed to me that he had chosen the one man in the Sect who could not afford to ignore it."

"Because I am guilty."

"Because you know what it costs to obey the Rule when the Rule is wrong."

Mu closes his eyes.

It has been a long time since anyone said it to his face.

* * *

He does it the hard way, because he knows no other.

He summons the Court's clerk, and the clerk of the Treasury, and the archivist of the Rule, and he sits them down one by one in the Law Pavilion with a brazier and a stack of vellum. He questions them as a magistrate questions: patiently, in order, without heat. He asks about the resolution of the spring. He asks about the amendment of Article forty-four. He asks who stood up in the Court and moved it, and who seconded, and who recorded the vote.

None of them remembers.

The Court's clerk, a lean sour woman of fifty, says she took the minutes herself. She produces them. They are in her hand. They record a resolution carried without dissent, in a session that, according to the attendance roll, was attended by four Elders and a quorum of two. She stares at the page for a long time.

"I do not recall this session," she says at last.

"Nor do I," says Mu. "Yet here is your hand."

"Here is my hand." She is gray. "I—Elder, I do not understand. I have never written a line I did not witness."

He looks at the paper in her fingers. He asks to see it. It is plum-bark: creamy, rough, slightly warm to the touch. He had not noticed. The Court has used mulberry paper for four hundred years. Someone has replaced a single leaf in the minute book, and no one saw the change.

Not a forgery, he thinks. A substitution.

A hand that could enter the Court archive, take out one sheet, write the minutes of a session that never happened, and put it back so smoothly that the clerk herself believed she had written it.

His skin tightens.

He dismisses her gently. He asks the archivist to bring him the Treasury's copy of the same minute, and it is, of course, in order.

* * *

The Rule is a cage, he thinks, standing at the window of the Law Pavilion in the long gold afternoon. The pool below is flat and bright. A cage, not a leash.

He had said it to himself so many times. He had said it on the day he signed the order in the yard. He had said it over seven years of nights. It had been true, in its way, and in being true it had let him sleep: I did not do it. The Rule did it. I was only the hand.

And now someone has used the cage.

Someone has taken the thing he loved and built a door in it. Someone has dictated a clause in the Rule, in his name and the Court's, against a man whom Mu himself, at the Council table, had once wanted to save. He had argued for the wedge. He had said, break the wall, take him in, make him ours. He had been outvoted, and thought it justice.

He sees now what he did not see then. He had not been defending the Rule. He had been defending his own idea of what it should do.

And the Rule has been used against him all the same.

What is the Rule, then? he thinks. What is it for, if it can be written by a man who does not exist?

He thinks of the Zhao girl in the yard. The Rule had said continue. He had continued. And three hours later, in the gray light, a man named Heng had come and taken the body, and said nothing, and looked at him with eyes in which there was no reproach at all.

He had wished, then, for reproach.

* * *

He goes to the training lawn before the sun is fully up.

He does not say why. The Law Pavilion's drill ground is a long strip of packed earth behind the cloister, and at this hour only one man is using it. Feng stands at the far end in shirt and leggings, barefoot on the frost, with a wooden practice sword held in a low guard. He does not hear Mu come. He is counting under his breath, in the slow low voice of a man who has done a thing ten thousand times and does not want to do it wrong on the ten thousand and first.

Mu watches from the edge.

The young man moves through a set of eleven forms. They are plain. They are Lin clan forms, shaped by a hand that has never had a master, and he knows half of them for what they are: the old Coral Gate basics, bent to fit an unlearned body. But there is no waste in them. Each cut ends where the next begins. Each step plants a heel and takes it up again without a sound. And in the quiet turn at the end of the set, when the blade stops a finger from the ground and the dawn light catches the edge, Mu feels the air tighten, the way it does in the presence of something that has learned to wait.

Foundation Middle, he thinks. At twenty-nine. From a mortal family with no sect line.

It is not impossible. It is not common either. The Sect's own Inner Court has twenty-two disciples of that standing, and every one of them had a patron, a pill budget, and a hall.

"Elder," says Feng, without turning. "You are standing in the wind."

"I am watching."

"I know. I could feel it." He lowers the blade. "You were counting my breath."

"Eleven to the minute. A slow rate."

"The Pill Hall says it should be nine." Feng smiles faintly. "I am working on it."

Mu steps onto the frost. He picks up the second practice sword from the rack, a plain white-oak thing weighted with lead, and turns it once in his hand. He has not held a sword for any purpose but ceremony in a long time.

"Come," he says. "One bout. No Qi."

"Elder—"

"Come."

They cross. It lasts perhaps a dozen breaths. Mu is a better swordsman; he is a Well-stage master with fifty years of forms behind him, and he sees every opening before it appears. But the young man does not give him the openings he expects. He gives him others. He takes the edge of the oak blade on his forearm and twists. He steps inside the guard. He puts his shoulder into Mu's ribs with a force that is not Qi but is not far from it, and Mu, who has not been put off his feet in thirty years, sits down on the frost.

For a moment he is merely surprised.

Then he laughs. It is a short, rusty sound, and neither of them knows what to do with it.

"Your brother taught you that," he says.

"My brother taught me to fall," says Feng. He offers his hand. "My father taught me to get up."

Mu takes the hand. It is dry and warm and callused. It does not shake.

"I would like," he says, standing, "to be able to say that I regret what was done. But it is not regret. I have had seven years to find the right word, and I cannot." He brushes the frost from his robe. "I know only that I will not let it be done again, in the Rule's name, to anyone."

"That will do," says Feng quietly. "For a start."

* * *

He confronts Zhou at noon, in the Treasury, because he cannot think of a reason not to.

The Elder of the Treasury sits at his desk beneath a wall of abacuses and tally-boards, with a bowl of pale tea at his elbow and a ledger open before him. He looks up at Mu's entrance with a round, mild, delighted smile that fades only by degrees.

"Mu, my friend. You never visit."

"I am here on the Court's business."

"Of course. Sit. Have tea." Zhou gestures, and his soft hand trembles, very slightly. "Is it the Gate Bearer? I have been sick about it, you know. A terrible business. A clever young man with a clever tongue. But the Rule is the Rule."

"Who proposed Article forty-four?"

The smile freezes.

"The Court proposed it."

"Which Elder?"

"I— it was a matter of general—" Zhou stops. He wets his lips. "You were there, Mu. You voted."

"I did not vote. There was no session." Mu does not raise his voice. "There was a leaf of plum-bark in the minute book, written in the clerk's hand. She does not remember the session. Neither do I."

The tea bowl is very still in its saucer.

"You are mistaken," says Zhou, and for the first time his voice goes high and thin. "You are tired. You have been under strain since the council. We have all been under strain. You mustn't—"

"Sixty silver a month, to the bearer."

Zhou stands.

It happens all at once. The chair goes back. The tea bowl rocks and spills. The round kind face is gray, then red, then gray again, and his hands are knotted in the sleeves of his robe, and his eyes, huge and wet, are fixed on a point just above Mu's shoulder as though someone were standing there.

"You do not know what you are protecting," he whispers.

"Tell me."

"I cannot." It comes out in a sob. "I cannot. They have my daughter's name. They had it before she was born. They have all of ours. You do not know what it is to open a door and find a ledger with your children's names in it, in an old man's handwriting, with the date of their birth in the margin, and a number, and a line that says not yet—"

"Zhou."

"Go away." He sinks back into the chair and covers his face. "Go away, Mu. Please. If they learn you came, they will take the child."

Mu looks at the bent head. Sixty years old. Soft hands. A man who has never done a thing he could not write down.

He thinks, with great clarity, This is what the cage was for. Not to keep the wolf out. To keep the sheep in.

He lays one hand briefly on the shaking shoulder. Then he turns and walks out of the Treasury into the light, and does not look back, and does not say a word to anyone about what he has seen.

* * *

The Arbiter receives him in the evening.

Shen Wuye is a lean dry man of eighty, with a cap of white hair and a mouth like a drawn knife. He sits in his bare study among shelves of vellum, and he does not rise. He listens to Mu in silence from beginning to end, his long fingers laced under his chin.

"You are asking me," he says, when it is done, "to suspend an amendment of the Rule on the word of a disciple under charge."

"I am asking you to inspect the minute book."

"And if the book is forged?"

"Then the Rule has been written by a hand outside the Sect." Mu's voice is hard. "And I will want to know whose."

"You are asking me to do a great deal."

"I am asking you to do your office." Mu leans forward. "The amendment was not carried. I have the Court's attendance roll. I have the clerk's confession that she does not remember the session. I have four Elders who deny moving it. I have the minute leaf, which is plum-bark, and which the Court has never used."

"A strange paper."

"The House's paper."

The Arbiter's fingers part. He stares at Mu for a long moment.

"You have said that name," he says slowly, "in this room."

"I have."

"It was not a name one said, when I was young." The old man looks suddenly very tired. "Forty years ago I thought it a story told to frighten clerks. A thing that kept the books of the books. I was told, when I took office, that there was nothing under the Rule. That the Rule was the floor."

"And now?"

"And now there is plum-bark in the minute book." Shen Wuye's mouth twists. "If I suspend Article forty-four on your word, Mu, I do so without proof. I will have to answer to the Council. I will have to answer to the Treasury. You will have to answer to the Court. And the suspension will be reversed in a month, because Zhou will bring forty witnesses to swear the session was held."

"Then suspend it for a month."

"For one month."

"A month is long enough." Mu rises. "The new moon is in three days."

The Arbiter looks at him.

"You are going to the Annex," he says.

"I am going with the Court's escort, under Article twelve, as the Gate Bearer requested." Mu's hand rests on the hilt at his belt. The reforged blade is cold under his fingers: Pool-grade, quiet, a gift from a forge he has not yet had the courage to thank. "I mean to open the door myself."

"And if there is nothing there?"

"Then I will have wronged an Elder of the Treasury, and I will resign my seat."

"And if there is something?"

For the first time in forty years, Mu does not have an answer ready.

* * *

On the night of the new moon the north terrace is dark.

There is no wind. There are no stars. A thin mist lies on the stones, and the lanterns carried by the escort make small, wavering circles in it that die at the edge of the light. Mu walks at the head of eight Court guards in the black of his office, his boots ringing, with Qin Hao a pace behind him and Feng at his left hand, bearing the Court's seal on a cord.

The guard on the stool at the end of the terrace has gone.

The stool is there. The lantern is there, burned to the wick. There is a half-whittled stick on the ground, and beside it a cup of cold tea. Mu bends and puts two fingers to the cup.

"Gone an hour," he says. "Perhaps less."

"They knew we were coming," says Qin Hao.

"They knew the hour. They did not know the name." Mu straightens. "Or they did, and judged it no longer worth the guard."

He walks the length of the building. Eight doors. All shut, and sealed with the plain gray wax of the Treasury. Mu breaks each seal in turn with his thumb and enters, one room after another, with the escort behind him. Old furniture. A stack of broken benches. A cabinet of unused scales. Rolls of felt. A heap of blankets gone gray with mildew. Seven rooms, seven smells of dust and damp wood.

The eighth is the one with the fourth number painted on the lintel.

He stops at the door. It is shut like the others. The seal is intact. But the wood around the latch is cold, colder than the night air, and when he lays his palm flat on it, it hums.

"Elder," says Qin Hao, at his shoulder, very low. "Do not."

"I have given my word."

"I know. I am only asking you to remember that you did." The Gate Elder's voice is rough. "Whatever is in there has been kept for a purpose. If the purpose was to be found by the Law—"

"Then the Law will find it."

Mu breaks the seal.

The door opens inward, without a creak, on a small bare room. There is a table. A lamp already lit, burning with a steady pale flame. And on the table, squared to its edge, a single book.

It is bound in plum-colored cloth. It lies open to a page. And on the page, in neat columns, in the same smooth even hand he has seen in the Court minute book, there is a list.

Numbers.

One column of numbers. Beside each, a name. A Sect name, in full, with a rank and a year. Some are crossed out. Some are not. He sees Zhou Mengyan, Treasury, Thirty-Six. He sees Pei, Hall of Weights, Ninety-Four. He sees names he knows, Elders, magistrates, a gate warden he drank with a dozen winters ago, and one by one they are marked with the same small cold figure.

He does not need to look for his own.

It is the seventh line from the bottom. In clear black ink, with a date beside it thirty-one years old.

MU DAOREN, Law, Forty-One.

Beside it, in the margin, in a different hand, a hand that is thin and spidery and very old, a single line is written, as if in reply to a question:

He will choose the Rule. He always has. Let him.

Mu stands very still.

Behind him, no one speaks. The lamp burns. The mist at the door coils and thins. And somewhere in the dark of the terrace, in the place where the hand that wrote the line has long since gone, he hears himself ask the only question left in the world:

Who entered me?
